cells.verb: keeping at the small daily work, by repetition, until it lives in your hands
cells.place: in the middle of an ending that has to finish before anything new can start
cells.ask: When the daily work shows you one thing you've been holding up that was never holding anything, let it come down in one go — and what comes back is practice that keeps you company instead of keeping you apart.
cells.core:
You're doing the small work every day, and it isn't costing you anything to do it. Something is ending around you and you're not fighting it or rushing it — you just keep showing up to the repetition, and the repetition is quietly clearing the ground. The time alone isn't a wall. People can still reach you in it.

That kind of steadiness earns a certain sight. Sooner or later it shows you a piece of the old arrangement that was never load-bearing — something you kept because it was there, not because it held. You're free to let that one fall all at once, cleanly, the way true things fall. Nothing about this asks you to; it's what the steadiness is for.
cells.sheetLine: You keep at the small work while the old thing ends, and the solitude still has people in it.

cells.tense: Future — bracing at an ending you keep refusing to let finish.
cells.verb: refining by repetition, now past the point where refining does anything
cells.place: at an ending that's already arrived and is waiting for you to stop polishing it
cells.ask: Set one thing down as finished before it's perfect, and leave it down — and what comes back is steadiness you choose instead of steadiness you cling to.
cells.core:
You're still sanding something that's already done. The ending happened; what you're doing now is making sure it ends flawlessly, and that's become a reason never to let it end at all. Somewhere ahead is a version where you finally got it right, and you're working toward that version instead of living in this one. The time alone has stopped being a choice. It's just where the work is, and you don't let yourself leave.

There's a fear under it about what happens the day you stop. Fair enough. But the thing you've been refining doesn't need another pass — it needs to be put down. One thing, this week, called finished while it still has a flaw you can see. Not giving up on it. Letting it be complete.
cells.sheetLine: You're perfecting an ending instead of letting it end.

cells.tense: Past — still standing at a door that already closed behind you.
cells.verb: picking up the small daily work, then dropping it before it has a chance to take
cells.place: on the far side of an ending, where the new thing is supposed to be getting built
cells.ask: Before you try again at the daily work, settle one lopsided account — give back one thing you owe, or take one thing you're owed, and let the exchange move — and what comes back is practice your hands actually want.
cells.core:
The old thing ended and the new one hasn't started, because starting means repeating something, and somewhere behind you repetition went badly. You begin, it gets uncomfortable in a familiar way, and you stop. Not from laziness — from memory. The door is shut and you're still answering to what was on the other side of it.

I'd leave the daily work alone for now. Pushing at an empty place only makes it emptier. The thing that's actually out of balance is what you give and what you get back — someone is carrying too much of this, or you are. Fix one piece of that, concretely. When the exchange is fair again, the steadiness tends to come back on its own, and it stops feeling like a trap.
cells.sheetLine: You can't stay with the small work because last time it cost you.

cells.tense: Disowned present — pen down in a room you're already writing in.
cells.verb: repeating the small work without ever calling it work
cells.place: inside an ending you turn out to be ready for
cells.ask: Guess the next step out loud before you know it's right, and notice whose hands already knew the way — and what comes back is practice you can finally claim, which is the only kind that stops being lonely.
cells.core:
You keep saying it just came together. The old arrangement is falling away and you're oddly ready for it — the skills are there, the timing is there — and you describe all of that as luck, or as the thing happening by itself. It isn't. The repetitions are being done. You just don't file them under practice, so the ending gets the credit and you don't.

Or the other way round: you're refusing the repetitions and calling that chance too. Either way, someone is steering. The way back isn't to look at the whole road; it's to take one step into what you can't see yet and watch how little you fumble. Your hands will tell you who's been practicing.
cells.sheetLine: You're practicing this ending. You call it luck.

flags.detail: "for years" — a cell knows no one's past
